events.title: Scuttling of the Graf Spee
events.blurb: A feared commerce-raider that had sunk nine merchant ships in three months limped into a neutral harbour for repairs after a running battle with three smaller cruisers, then sat immobile while international diplomacy set a 72-hour countdown. Twenty thousand spectators lined the waterfront to watch her captain make his final decision.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1939, Montevideo. Captain Hans Langsdorff scuttled the Admiral Graf Spee at 8:55 PM rather than risk his crew in what he believed was an overwhelming British trap. Three days later he wrapped himself in the ship's battle ensign and shot himself. The trap was largely bluff.

events.title: Battle of Crete
events.blurb: For the first time in military history, an entire island was invaded and captured primarily by paratroopers and glider-borne troops alone, dropped onto an enemy-held coastline in the face of fierce resistance. The attackers suffered such catastrophic losses on the opening day that the tactic was never repeated at this scale.
events.revealBlurb: May 20 – June 1, 1941 — Operation Mercury. German paratroopers suffered over 6,500 casualties, including roughly 3,000 killed. Hitler was so shaken he banned future mass airborne operations. The British, Australian, and New Zealand defenders were evacuated; 5,000 were left behind and taken prisoner.

events.title: Warsaw Uprising
events.blurb: A resistance army launched an all-out urban insurrection timed to coincide with an approaching allied army's arrival at the city's eastern bank, intending to liberate the capital before that army entered — but the expected support never came, leaving 40,000 fighters and 200,000 civilians to a 63-day battle against overwhelming force that ended in total destruction.
events.revealBlurb: August 1 – October 2, 1944. The Polish Home Army rose at 5:00 PM on August 1 with roughly 40,000 fighters. The approaching Soviet Army halted on the opposite bank and waited. Stalin also denied Allied planes permission to use Soviet airfields for supply drops for weeks. An estimated 200,000 civilians were killed; survivors were expelled and the city was systematically demolished.

events.title: Battle of Okinawa
events.blurb: 180,000 American troops landed on an island 350 miles from the Japanese home islands on Easter Sunday, triggering the largest amphibious assault in the Pacific and the longest land battle of that theatre — 82 days of cave-to-cave fighting, mass suicide charges, and the heaviest naval losses the United States suffered in any single campaign.
events.revealBlurb: April 1 – June 22, 1945. US casualties: roughly 12,000 killed and 36,000 wounded. Japanese military deaths: over 110,000. An estimated 100,000 Okinawan civilians also died. The kamikaze campaign sank 36 US ships and damaged 368. American planners, projecting similar resistance during a home-island invasion, estimated 1 million US casualties — a figure that influenced the decision to use atomic bombs.

events.title: Death of Hitler
events.blurb: The dictator who had triggered the continent's most destructive conflict, directed the murder of millions, and sworn never to be taken alive shot himself in a subterranean command centre beneath a capital city now surrounded by enemy armies, having married his companion the previous day and designated a naval admiral as his successor.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1945 — Hitler shot himself at approximately 3:30 PM in the Führerbunker; Eva Braun took cyanide. Their bodies were carried to the garden and burned. By explicit prior order, no intact corpse was to fall into enemy hands. Soviet forces found the remains eight days after the surrender; Stalin kept the truth of their forensic identification secret for decades.

events.title: Justinian's Code Issued
events.blurb: A Byzantine emperor's commission of ten jurists, working for 14 months, compiled nearly a thousand years of Roman legal rulings into a single four-part code. It became the foundation of civil-law systems across continental Europe and, centuries later, Latin America. Imperial-era laws contradicted themselves; the code resolved the contradictions by fiat.
events.revealBlurb: April 7, 529 — Emperor Justinian I issued the first edition. The final compilation, called the Corpus Juris Civilis, influenced the Napoleonic Code and every legal system modeled on it. Law students still read excerpts today.

events.title: Battle of Tours
events.blurb: A Frankish mayor of the palace led an infantry army into a defensive wall of shields against a much larger Umayyad cavalry force that had been raiding deep into western Europe. The battle's outcome stopped the northward expansion of the Islamic caliphate into the Frankish heartland and established the Carolingian dynasty as the dominant power of the region.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 732 — Charles Martel ("Charles the Hammer") in central France. His grandson Charlemagne would be crowned emperor 68 years later. Edward Gibbon later wrote that without the victory, "the interpretation of the Koran would now be taught in the schools of Oxford."

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: Battle of Legnica
events.blurb: A Mongol detachment under a grandson of Genghis Khan annihilated a combined Polish, Silesian, and Templar army in a field southwest of a town in Lower Silesia, killing a duke and most of his knights. The defeat should have opened central Europe to full Mongol conquest. Instead, news reached the army that the Great Khan in distant Karakorum had died, and the generals withdrew to attend the succession.
events.revealBlurb: April 9, 1241 — Mongol commander Orda. The Mongols traditionally displayed the severed right ears of the dead to count the slain; sources claim they filled nine large sacks. Europe was saved by Mongol electoral politics, not European arms.

events.title: Black Death Reaches Europe
events.blurb: A plague arriving by trade galley at a Sicilian port spread through Mediterranean shipping lanes and overland caravans until, over the next five years, it killed an estimated 30-60 percent of Europe's population — perhaps 50 million people. Physicians had no effective response; flagellant processions and mass pogroms of Jews did little but spread the disease faster.
events.revealBlurb: October 1347 — Messina, Sicily. Caused by Yersinia pestis, spread by the fleas of black rats. Wages for surviving laborers roughly doubled; labor scarcity began eroding feudal obligations. The plague cycled back every decade or so for the next three centuries.

events.title: Transistor Invented
events.blurb: Three physicists at an American industrial research laboratory demonstrated a working point-contact transistor — a tiny semiconductor device made from germanium that could amplify electrical signals without the vacuum tubes, heat, and bulk then required. Within a decade the invention had reshaped electronics; within five decades, billions of its descendants would fit on a single silicon chip smaller than a fingernail.
events.revealBlurb: December 23, 1947 — John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley at Bell Labs. They shared the 1956 Nobel. Shockley's later semiconductor company, though commercially a failure, seeded Silicon Valley through the departure of its "Traitorous Eight" founders of Fairchild Semiconductor.

events.title: Intel 4004 Microprocessor Released
events.blurb: Intel released a 4-bit central processing unit containing 2,300 transistors on a silicon chip the size of a fingernail, capable of 60,000 operations per second. Originally designed for a Japanese calculator company, it became the world's first commercially available microprocessor — the prototype for every CPU that followed.

events.title: Microsoft Founded
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore and his 22-year-old friend, working out of a cheap room in an Albuquerque motel, formally established a partnership to develop software for microcomputers. Their first product had been a BASIC interpreter for the Altair 8800, licensed to the kit's manufacturer. The contract paid royalties per machine sold. Within seven years they would own the personal-computer operating system industry.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1975 — Bill Gates and Paul Allen. Originally "Micro-Soft." They moved to the Seattle suburb of Bellevue in 1979 and to Redmond in 1986. Allen left the company in 1983 after being diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma; he recovered, founded other businesses, died in 2018.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: iPad Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company released a 9.7-inch tablet — something between a smartphone and a laptop — running the same operating system as its phone. The product's name had been mocked in advance for rhyming with certain feminine-hygiene products; the device itself went on to redefine a computing form factor that previous attempts by Microsoft and others had never managed to make stick. It sold 3 million units in its first 80 days.
events.revealBlurb: April 3, 2010 — Apple iPad. Steve Jobs' last major product launch. "I think we have a winner here," he said at the introduction. Microsoft's Bill Gates had been pushing tablet PCs for a decade; Apple's combination of software, battery, and price finally made the form factor work.

events.title: NATO Founded
events.blurb: Twelve nations from both sides of the Atlantic signed a mutual defense treaty in Washington, D.C., committing that an armed attack against one would be considered an attack against all. The alliance was built around Article 5 — a collective defense clause that has been invoked exactly once in its history, after 9/11.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1949 — founding members included the US, UK, France, Canada, and eight others. Lord Ismay, its first Secretary General, quipped its purpose was "to keep the Russians out, the Americans in, and the Germans down."

events.title: Helsinki Accords
events.blurb: Thirty-five nations — every European country except tiny Albania, plus the U.S. and Canada — signed a sweeping final act in the Finnish capital that acknowledged post-war borders while binding signatories to respect human rights. Critics called it a sellout to Moscow. In fact, its human rights provisions gave eastern dissidents a legal framework that would undermine the regimes a decade later.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 1975 — the "Third Basket" on human rights proved subversive. Czech dissidents founded Charter 77 using its language; the Moscow Helsinki Group followed. Brezhnev didn't realize he'd just signed his system's eventual death warrant.

events.title: "Evil Empire" Speech
events.blurb: Addressing the National Association of Evangelicals in Florida, a U.S. president abandoned the detente rhetoric of his predecessors and described the rival superpower as "the focus of evil in the modern world." Speechwriters had lifted the phrase from a Star Wars reference. The framing shocked diplomats but reflected a deeper strategy: rhetorically delegitimize the opponent rather than coexist with it.
events.revealBlurb: March 8, 1983 — Ronald Reagan in Orlando. Speechwriter Tony Dolan had sneaked "evil empire" past the State Department, which had deleted it from earlier drafts. Two weeks later Reagan announced the Strategic Defense Initiative.

events.title: Chernobyl Disaster
events.blurb: During a safety test at the No. 4 reactor of a Ukrainian nuclear power plant, a power surge, flawed reactor design, and operator errors combined to blow the 1,000-tonne reactor lid off the building and send a radioactive plume across Europe. Swedish sensors detected the contamination before Moscow admitted anything had happened. The exclusion zone around the plant remains largely uninhabited nearly forty years on.
events.revealBlurb: April 26, 1986 — 1:23 AM. Two workers died in the initial explosion; 28 firefighters and operators died of acute radiation poisoning in the months after. Roughly 350,000 people were permanently evacuated. Cleanup cost the USSR an estimated 18 billion rubles.

events.title: "Tear Down This Wall" Speech
events.blurb: Speaking in front of the Brandenburg Gate in a divided German city, a U.S. president issued a direct public challenge to the Soviet leader: "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!" The State Department had tried to cut the line from the draft four times, considering it inflammatory. The president insisted. Twenty-eight months later, the wall fell.
events.revealBlurb: June 12, 1987 — Reagan in West Berlin. The phrase went mostly unremarked at the time; American newspapers buried it. Its posthumous fame owes more to the actual wall's 1989 collapse than to anything it said in the moment.

events.title: Rubik's Cube Global Craze
events.blurb: A 3×3 mechanical puzzle cube invented six years earlier by a Hungarian architecture professor became a global bestseller after licensed international distribution began. Over 100 million units sold in the first three years. Books of solutions appeared on bestseller lists. The puzzle's simplicity — six colours, 43 quintillion possible states, a single solved configuration — caught people who had never bought a toy in their lives. World championships began in 1982.
events.revealBlurb: 1981 — Ernő Rubik had patented the cube in 1975; it went international in 1980. The first world championship was in Budapest, June 5, 1982; the current world record for solving it is under 3.05 seconds (Max Park, June 2023). The cube remains in continuous production.

events.title: New Coke Launched
events.blurb: A 99-year-old American beverage company launched a reformulated version of its flagship cola, sweeter and smoother, aimed at winning back market share from Pepsi in a rivalry called the Cola Wars. Blind taste tests had shown a preference for the new recipe; actual consumer response, once they knew what they were drinking, was widespread rage. Letters of protest poured into Atlanta; soda fountains advertised the return of the original. 79 days later, the company announced the comeback of "Coca-Cola Classic."
events.revealBlurb: April 23, 1985 — Coca-Cola. The original formula returned as "Coca-Cola Classic" on July 11, 1985. New Coke eventually became "Coke II" in 1992 and was quietly discontinued in 2002. The whole episode is now a business-school case study in consumer-brand attachment.

events.title: Kurt Cobain Dies
events.blurb: A 27-year-old grunge-rock frontman was found dead of a self-inflicted shotgun wound in the greenhouse above the garage of his Seattle home. He had struggled with heroin addiction, a collapsed marriage, chronic stomach pain, and the deep anxieties of sudden fame. His suicide note quoted a line from a Neil Young song: "It's better to burn out than to fade away." A public memorial at Seattle Center drew 7,000 mourners.
events.revealBlurb: April 5, 1994 — Kurt Cobain of Nirvana. The body was not discovered for three days, by an electrician installing a security system. Conspiracy theories have persisted for decades. Cobain joined the "27 Club" of pop musicians who died at that age, including Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, Jim Morrison, and Amy Winehouse.

events.title: Princess Diana Dies
events.blurb: A 36-year-old former British princess and two others died in a high-speed car crash in an underpass in central Paris after their driver attempted to evade pursuing paparazzi. Her death — ten months after her divorce from the heir to the British throne — triggered a massive public outpouring of grief that caught the British monarchy off guard. Over a million bouquets of flowers were left at London's royal palaces. Her funeral a week later was watched by 2.5 billion people globally.
events.revealBlurb: August 31, 1997 — Diana, Princess of Wales at the Pont de l'Alma tunnel. Her companion Dodi Fayed and the drunk driver Henri Paul also died; bodyguard Trevor Rees-Jones survived. Elton John performed a rewritten "Candle in the Wind" at the funeral, which became the best-selling single of all time.

events.title: Seinfeld Finale
events.blurb: The 180th and final episode of a nine-year NBC sitcom about petty New York narcissists aired to 76 million viewers. The divisive finale had the four main characters put on trial in a fictional Massachusetts town for failing to help a carjacking victim, watched by a parade of minor characters from earlier seasons who had been wronged by them. Critics and fans were largely disappointed; its creator defended it as consistent with the show's amoral premise.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1998 — "The Finale." Written by Larry David, returning after leaving the show in 1996. Ad slots on the finale sold for around $2 million for 30 seconds — a pre-Super Bowl record for a TV program.

events.title: FIFA Founded
events.blurb: Representatives of seven European national football associations — Belgium, Denmark, France, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland — met at a Paris sports association's offices and established an international governing body for the sport. England, which had invented the modern codified game and considered itself the natural authority, declined to attend, joined in 1905, and withdrew multiple times over subsequent decades in petty disputes. The organization would run the World Cup from 1930 on.
events.revealBlurb: May 21, 1904 — Fédération Internationale de Football Association, Paris. Its first president was Robert Guérin. FIFA now has 211 member associations, more than the UN. Its headquarters moved to Zurich in 1932 and have been there since.

events.title: Battle of the Sexes Tennis Match
events.blurb: A 29-year-old professional tennis player defeated a 55-year-old former Wimbledon champion in straight sets before a crowd of 30,000 at the Houston Astrodome and a television audience of 90 million. The retired player had publicly declared that no woman could defeat him, offering a $100,000 prize to any who tried.

events.title: Hank Aaron Breaks Ruth's Record
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Atlanta outfielder hit his 715th career home run off a Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher, breaking Babe Ruth's 39-year-old career record in front of a sellout home crowd. He had endured a year of death threats, racist mail, and FBI protection as he approached the record. As he rounded second base, two white college students ran onto the field alongside him — security later decided they had meant only to escort him. He tipped his cap as he crossed home plate.
events.revealBlurb: April 8, 1974 — Hank Aaron at Atlanta-Fulton County Stadium, off Al Downing. His final career total was 755 home runs, which stood as the record until Barry Bonds passed it in 2007. The FBI had warned him that multiple credible plots to assassinate him were active that season.

events.title: Tiger Woods Wins First Masters
events.blurb: A 21-year-old American golfer, playing in his first Masters as a professional, won the prestigious Augusta tournament by 12 strokes — the largest margin in the event's history — with a record-setting 18-under-par total. He was the youngest winner of a Masters, the first with African ancestry, and the first of Asian heritage. The club had admitted its first Black member only seven years earlier. Viewership had doubled the previous year's; his arrival reshaped the demographics, marketing, and money of professional golf.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1997 — Tiger Woods at Augusta National. He would win 15 major championships across a career including three more Masters wins. His dominance of the sport from 1997 through 2008 has been widely called one of the most influential individual runs in professional sports.

events.title: Kobe Bryant Dies
events.blurb: A 41-year-old retired basketball star, his 13-year-old daughter, and seven other passengers died when their private helicopter crashed into a hillside in thick fog outside Los Angeles while en route to a youth basketball game. The retired player had won five NBA championships, two Olympic golds, and the nickname "Black Mamba" during a 20-year career entirely with the Los Angeles Lakers. The crash prompted an outpouring of mourning around the world.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 2020 — Kobe and Gianna Bryant. National Transportation Safety Board findings attributed the crash to pilot error in poor visibility. His 2017 jersey-retirement ceremony at Staples Center saw both his numbers (8 and 24) raised to the rafters — the only player in franchise history with multiple retired numbers.

events.title: Monroe Doctrine Declared
events.blurb: An American president's annual address to Congress warned European powers against further colonization or political interference in the Western Hemisphere, a policy the United States could not yet militarily enforce but would cite for the next two centuries. The message was drafted largely by his Secretary of State, a future president himself.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1823 — James Monroe. The phrase "Monroe Doctrine" wasn't coined until 1850. Britain quietly backed the policy because it suited their own trade interests, and for decades the Royal Navy did most of the actual enforcing.

events.title: Confederate Attack on Fort Sumter
events.blurb: At 4:30 in the morning, Confederate artillery opened fire on the federal garrison at Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, beginning a 34-hour bombardment that forced the Union to surrender and formally launched the deadliest war in American history. No one was killed in the bombardment itself — two Union soldiers died in a cannon accident during the surrender ceremony.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1861 — Charleston, South Carolina. The Confederacy fired over 4,000 shells at the fort; Union defenders fired roughly 1,000 back. Nobody died in combat during the entire engagement. Within four days, President Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers, and four more states seceded to join the Confederacy.

events.title: Abraham Lincoln Assassinated
events.blurb: At approximately 10:15 pm that night — five days after Confederate General Robert E. Lee surrendered at Appomattox — actor and Confederate sympathizer John Wilkes Booth shot President Abraham Lincoln in the head at Ford's Theatre in Washington. Lincoln never regained consciousness and died at 7:22 the following morning; he was the first American president to be assassinated.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 1865 — Ford's Theatre, Washington, D.C. Booth coordinated simultaneous attacks on Vice President Johnson and Secretary of State Seward the same night; both failed. Lincoln's bodyguard had left his post to watch the play from a better vantage point.

events.title: Apollo 1 Launchpad Fire
events.blurb: During a ground test at Cape Kennedy that afternoon, a fire broke out inside the Apollo 1 command module, killing all three crew members — Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee — in less than a minute. The cause was an electrical spark in an atmosphere of pure oxygen at elevated pressure, and the hatch could not be opened quickly enough to save anyone.
events.revealBlurb: January 27, 1967 — Launch Complex 34, Cape Kennedy, Florida. The crew could not escape because the hatch required 90 seconds to open inward — and the fire created pressure that made it impossible to swing. The disaster set the Moon program back 20 months but ultimately produced a safer spacecraft.

events.title: Bush v. Gore Halts Florida Recount
events.blurb: The Supreme Court ruled 5–4 to halt the manual recount of Florida's contested presidential ballots, effectively awarding the state's 25 electoral votes to Republican George W. Bush and deciding the closest presidential election since 1876. The margin in Florida's certified count was 537 votes out of nearly 6 million cast; Al Gore ultimately conceded, and Bush won the presidency 271–266 in the Electoral College.
events.revealBlurb: December 12, 2000 — Washington, D.C. The per curiam opinion included the extraordinary disclaimer that the ruling "is limited to the present circumstances" and should not be treated as precedent. The butterfly ballot design in Palm Beach County alone may have cost Gore 2,000–3,000 votes to Pat Buchanan.

events.title: Jackie Robinson Breaks Color Barrier
events.blurb: A 28-year-old second baseman took the field at a Brooklyn ballpark and became the first African-American to play in modern Major League Baseball, breaking a 63-year color line enforced by gentlemen's agreement rather than written rule. He went hitless in his debut but reached base on an error and scored the winning run.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1947 — Ebbets Field, Brooklyn Dodgers. Team president Branch Rickey had signed him with the understanding he would absorb abuse without retaliation for two years. Robinson's number 42 was retired across every MLB team in 1997, the only such universal retirement in sports.

events.title: Emmett Till Murdered
events.blurb: A 14-year-old Black boy visiting family in a rural Southern state was abducted from his great-uncle's home in the middle of the night, tortured, shot, and thrown into a river with a cotton-gin fan tied around his neck. His mother insisted on an open-casket funeral so the world could see what had been done to her son. Photographs of the mutilated body, published in Jet magazine, galvanized a generation.
events.revealBlurb: August 28, 1955 — Money, Mississippi. His accuser, Carolyn Bryant, admitted decades later she had lied about the encounter. Her husband and his half-brother were acquitted by an all-white jury, then sold their confession to Look magazine knowing they couldn't be retried.

events.title: Black Panther Party Founded
events.blurb: Two community-college students in a California Bay Area city drafted a ten-point program demanding full employment, decent housing, exemption from military service, and an end to police brutality for Black Americans. They organized armed neighborhood patrols to monitor police, opened free-breakfast programs for children, and ran medical clinics. The FBI declared them "the greatest threat to internal security" within four years.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 1966 — Huey Newton and Bobby Seale in Oakland. J. Edgar Hoover's COINTELPRO infiltrated the party and fabricated rivalries between it and the US Organization; the free breakfasts, which he called "the greatest threat," fed 20,000 children a day at their peak.

events.title: Thurgood Marshall Confirmed
events.blurb: The U.S. Senate confirmed the first African-American justice of the Supreme Court by a vote of 69-11 after a contentious hearing in which Southern senators grilled him on obscure constitutional questions in an effort to embarrass him. He had already argued 32 cases before the Court — and won 29 — as the NAACP's lead attorney. He served 24 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 30, 1967 — confirmed to replace Tom Clark. Lyndon Johnson had said bluntly on tape: "I want folks to look up and see a Negro lawyer up there." Marshall was the grandson of a slave and had been rejected by the University of Maryland law school on racial grounds.

events.title: Martin Luther King Jr. Assassinated
events.blurb: Stepping onto the balcony outside Room 306 of a Tennessee motel where he was staying while supporting a sanitation workers' strike, the country's most prominent civil rights leader was shot once with a high-powered rifle from across the street. He died an hour later at a nearby hospital. He was 39. Riots broke out in more than 100 American cities within hours of the news.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1968 — Lorraine Motel, Memphis. His killer, escaped convict James Earl Ray, was captured in London two months later. The night before, King had ended a speech with: "I've been to the mountaintop. I may not get there with you, but we, as a people, will get to the Promised Land."

events.title: Plato's Republic
events.blurb: An Athenian philosopher completed a ten-book Socratic dialogue in which his deceased teacher argues with several interlocutors about the nature of justice and, by extension, the ideal city. The work would become the foundational text of Western political philosophy; its allegory of the cave, its philosopher-king proposal, and its ban on poets have been quoted, contested, and imitated ever since.
events.revealBlurb: c. 380 BCE — Plato. Alfred North Whitehead famously called European philosophy "a series of footnotes to Plato." The Republic was unknown in the medieval Latin West until the Renaissance; it reached Islamic and Byzantine scholars first.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Les Misérables Published
events.blurb: A 60-year-old French novelist living in exile on the Channel Island of Guernsey published a 1,500-page five-volume novel tracing the arc of a paroled convict redeeming himself over decades, set against the 1832 June Rebellion in Paris. He had been working on it, off and on, for seventeen years. The publisher sent the first volume simultaneously to seven European capitals; the author paid for advertising out of his own pocket. It was an instant international sensation.
events.revealBlurb: April 3, 1862 — Victor Hugo. The famous shortest correspondence in literary history happened around this book: Hugo, on holiday, wired his publisher "?" — the reply came back "!" — confirming strong sales.

events.title: Treasure Island Published
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Scottish writer, suffering severe pulmonary illness and convalescing in the Scottish Highlands, sketched a treasure map with his 12-year-old stepson on a rainy afternoon and began improvising a story for the boy. The serialized pirate adventure novel that grew from the map — featuring a peg-legged cook, a squawking parrot, a buried fortune, and a black spot — essentially defined the iconography of piracy for the next century and a half.
events.revealBlurb: November 14, 1883 — Robert Louis Stevenson. Initially serialized in the magazine Young Folks in 1881 as "The Sea Cook." The phrase "Shiver me timbers!" does not appear in the book but was popularized by its Long John Silver.

events.title: The Great Gatsby Published
events.blurb: A 28-year-old American novelist published his third novel — a 218-page story about a wealthy bootlegger's obsessive love for an old flame now married to a brutish Yale football star, narrated by a Midwestern newcomer to Long Island. Reviews were respectable; sales were tepid. The author died 15 years later considering himself a failure. The book was rediscovered during WWII when Armed Services Editions shipped 155,000 copies to U.S. soldiers; it is now read in every American high school.
events.revealBlurb: April 10, 1925 — F. Scott Fitzgerald. Original print run: 20,870 copies. Fitzgerald earned $200 in royalties from his fourth novel "Tender Is the Night." His high-schooler daughter Scottie, who detested "The Great Gatsby," left her father's papers to Princeton.

events.title: Euclid's Elements Written
events.blurb: A 13-book mathematical treatise organised geometry, number theory, and proportion into a rigorous deductive system built from five simple axioms and five postulates, from which hundreds of theorems were derived by logical proof alone. The work became the model for mathematical reasoning for more than two thousand years and remained a standard university textbook in parts of Europe into the twentieth century.
events.revealBlurb: c. 300 BCE — almost nothing is known about Euclid himself; even his birthdate is unknown. The Elements is the second most-printed book in history after the Bible. One of its five postulates — the parallel postulate — resisted proof for two thousand years; mathematicians who tried to derive it instead invented non-Euclidean geometry.

events.title: On the Origin of Species Published
events.blurb: A 502-page book argued that all species of life descended from common ancestors through a process of natural selection, where individuals with heritable traits better suited to their environment survived and reproduced at higher rates. The first print run of 1,250 copies sold out to booksellers on the day it was offered for sale.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1859 — Darwin had sat on the theory for twenty years, terrified of the controversy. He finally rushed it to press only after Alfred Russel Wallace independently wrote him a letter describing the same mechanism. The two men's papers were presented jointly to the Linnean Society in 1858.

events.title: Hubble Shows Universe Is Expanding
events.blurb: An astronomer compiled measurements of twenty-three galaxies and demonstrated that distant galaxies are receding from us at speeds proportional to their distance — the farther away, the faster the recession. The pattern implied the universe had a beginning point and was still growing in every direction, a result that forced a fundamental rethink of cosmology and was initially resisted by most physicists.
events.revealBlurb: March 15, 1929 — much of the raw redshift data Hubble used was collected by Vesto Slipher and Henrietta Swan Leavitt, neither of whom shared the credit. The "Hubble Constant" measuring the expansion rate is still disputed by modern astronomers; different measurement methods give slightly different answers.

events.title: Human Genome Project Completed
events.blurb: An international consortium announced the completion of a map of the entire 3-billion-letter chemical sequence of human DNA, covering 99 percent of gene-containing regions at 99.99 percent accuracy — two years ahead of schedule. The project, begun in 1990, required coordinating laboratories across six countries and produced a reference sequence that has underpinned virtually every major advance in genetic medicine since.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 2003 — a rival private effort by Celera Genomics, led by Craig Venter, raced the public consortium and forced both teams to declare a joint "completion" in 2000. The actual finished sequence was only completed in 2003. A truly gapless human genome wasn't assembled until 2022, when long-read sequencing technology filled the remaining 8%.

events.title: First Black Hole Image Captured
events.blurb: A global network of radio telescopes, coordinated to act as a single Earth-sized dish, produced the first direct image of a black hole's event horizon — a glowing ring of superheated gas surrounding a dark central void at the centre of a galaxy 55 million light-years away. Processing the petabytes of data required a custom algorithm developed in part by a graduate student whose contribution went initially unrecognised.
events.revealBlurb: April 10, 2019 — the black hole in galaxy M87 is 6.5 billion times the mass of the Sun. Katie Bouman, then a postdoc, developed much of the imaging algorithm and became briefly internet-famous when a photo of her looking at the result on a laptop went viral. The press release was coordinated across six cities in six time zones simultaneously.

events.title: Mount Tambora Eruption
events.blurb: A volcano on an Indonesian island blew its top in the most powerful eruption in recorded history, spewing 150 cubic kilometres of material into the atmosphere. The sulphate aerosols lingered in the stratosphere for years, cooling global temperatures by roughly a degree and producing crop failures, famine, and snow in June across the northern hemisphere the following year.
events.revealBlurb: April 10, 1815 — Mount Tambora on Sumbawa, Indonesia. 1816 became "the year without a summer." Mary Shelley, trapped indoors by endless rain in Switzerland, wrote Frankenstein. J.M.W. Turner's lurid sunsets from the decade owe their color to Tambora's dust.

events.title: San Francisco Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake ripped a 477-kilometre tear through the fault running up the California coast, hitting a West Coast boom city just after 5 AM. The shaking was severe, but the four-day fire that followed — fed by broken gas mains and fought with limited water from shattered pipes — did most of the damage, destroying 80 percent of the city and killing around 3,000.
events.revealBlurb: April 18, 1906 — San Francisco. The mayor authorized dynamiting buildings to create firebreaks; most of the dynamiting actually spread the fire. The opera singer Enrico Caruso, in town for a performance, vowed never to return. He didn't.

events.title: Great Kantō Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck the main Japanese island at noon, as hundreds of thousands of households were preparing lunch over charcoal braziers. The fires that erupted in the collapsed wooden city were fanned by a typhoon passing offshore, merging into a single firestorm with tornadoes of flame. Around 140,000 people died; 1.9 million were left homeless.
events.revealBlurb: September 1, 1923 — Tokyo and Yokohama. A persistent false rumor that ethnic Koreans were poisoning wells led to vigilante massacres of some 6,000 Korean residents. September 1 is now Japan's Disaster Prevention Day.

events.title: Indian Ocean Tsunami
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the western coast of Sumatra — the third-largest ever recorded — displaced so much water that tsunami waves up to 30 metres high raced across the Indian Ocean, hitting 14 countries within hours. Around 228,000 people died in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand, and as far away as Somalia. No warning system existed.
events.revealBlurb: December 26, 2004 — Boxing Day. A 10-year-old British girl named Tilly Smith recognized the receding tide from a school geography lesson and got her family's Phuket beach evacuated, saving around 100 lives. A basin-wide warning system was operational by 2006.

events.title: Sichuan Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake struck a mountainous province of southwest China in the mid-afternoon, killing around 87,000 people, including thousands of schoolchildren when substandard school buildings collapsed while adjacent government offices stood intact. The "tofu construction" scandal triggered rare citizen protests that were sharply suppressed.
events.revealBlurb: May 12, 2008 — Sichuan Province, three months before the Beijing Olympics. An artist named Ai Weiwei spent years compiling the names of the dead children; his office was raided and he was detained.

events.title: First Human in Orbit
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Soviet Air Force pilot rode a modified intercontinental ballistic missile into a single orbit reaching 327 km altitude, completing one lap of Earth in 108 minutes before ejecting from his capsule at 7 km and parachuting separately to a field in southern Russia. The mission was fully automated; Gagarin held an emergency manual-control key sealed in an envelope in case he needed it.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1961 — Vostok 1. Gagarin was chosen partly because he was 1.57 m tall and fit the cramped capsule. He shouted "Poyekhali!" ("Let's go!") at liftoff — the same casual phrase Russian pilots use to start any flight. The module didn't fully separate and sent him spinning at 8 Gs before a wire bundle burned through.

events.title: First Soft Moon Landing
events.blurb: The Soviet Luna 9 spacecraft landed intact on the Ocean of Storms, becoming the first vehicle to achieve a controlled soft landing on another world and transmit photographs from the surface. Its four petal-shaped panels opened to right the lander and deploy an antenna, then it sent back a panoramic image sequence over three sessions totaling nine images.
events.revealBlurb: February 3, 1966 — Luna 9. British radio astronomers at Jodrell Bank intercepted the transmission and noticed it used the same format as a standard wire-photo machine. They borrowed a Müller facsimile unit from a news agency and published the images before the Soviets released them officially — to Moscow's considerable irritation.

events.title: Apollo 13 Oxygen Tank Rupture
events.blurb: An oxygen tank in the Apollo 13 Service Module exploded 56 hours into the mission, venting both oxygen tanks to space and forcing the crew to abandon the Command Module for the Lunar Module, which was designed to support two people for two days but kept three alive for four. The crew looped around the Moon and returned safely after improvising a CO₂ scrubber from materials aboard using instructions radioed from Earth.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1970 — Apollo 13. The tank that exploded had been accidentally dropped during ground testing 18 months earlier. Mission controllers in Houston coined "successful failure" to describe the outcome. The crew consumed so little water during the return that all three were severely dehydrated; Lovell lost 6.5 kg.

events.title: Grand Tour Launch
events.blurb: A Titan IIIE rocket launched a 722-kilogram probe carrying a gold-plated phonograph record with greetings in 55 languages and 116 images. Its trajectory used gravitational assists from Jupiter and Saturn to reach escape velocity.

events.title: First American Woman in Space
events.blurb: Physicist Sally Ride flew aboard Space Shuttle Challenger as a mission specialist on STS-7, becoming the first American woman and the youngest American in space at 32. The six-day mission deployed two communications satellites and was the first shuttle flight to use a robotic arm to retrieve a free-flying satellite.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1983 — STS-7. A reporter asked Ride before launch whether spaceflight would affect her reproductive organs; she deadpanned that no one had asked her male crewmates the same question. NASA engineers reportedly asked whether 100 tampons would be enough for the six-day flight "just to be safe." She flew again in 1984 and co-founded a science education company.

events.title: Handel's Messiah Premieres
events.blurb: A 57-year-old German-born, London-resident composer conducted the premiere of a three-hour oratorio he had written in 24 days, at a charity concert in a hall in an Irish capital. Ladies were asked not to wear hoops and gentlemen not to wear swords so more could fit in the venue. The proceeds benefited a hospital, a prison society, and a charitable infirmary. Two of the inmates were released on the night using the concert's proceeds.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1742 — George Frideric Handel at the Great Music Hall on Fishamble Street, Dublin. The "Hallelujah Chorus" became a standing-ovation custom. It's rumored King George II stood at its London premiere; no contemporary source confirms the story.

events.title: Louis Armstrong's Hot Fives
events.blurb: A 24-year-old cornetist who had grown up in the poorest section of New Orleans walked into a Chicago studio for the first session with a small band of his own. Over the next three years, the "Hot Five" and "Hot Seven" sessions would reshape popular music. His vocal improvisation on "Heebie Jeebies" — a chorus of nonsense syllables when he claimed to drop his lyric sheet — launched scat singing. His trumpet solos made the individual improvisation the heart of jazz.
events.revealBlurb: November 12, 1925 — Louis Armstrong at OKeh Records, Chicago. The "Heebie Jeebies" vocal made him a national figure. He would become the first African-American to host a nationally sponsored radio show.

events.title: Strange Fruit Recorded
events.blurb: A 23-year-old African-American singer, in a Manhattan studio, recorded a song about the lynching of Black Americans that had been written by a Jewish high-school teacher from the Bronx. Her regular label refused to release it; a tiny specialty label agreed. She closed with it at every set at her Greenwich Village club, the room going dark except for a spotlight on her face, no encore permitted. The song haunted her for the rest of her short life.
events.revealBlurb: April 20, 1939 — Billie Holiday, Commodore Records. Songwriter: Abel Meeropol, under the pen name Lewis Allan. Meeropol and his wife later adopted the two young sons of the executed Ethel and Julius Rosenberg.

events.title: Woodstock Festival
events.blurb: A three-day music festival, overcapacity within hours of opening, drew an estimated 400,000 young people to a dairy farm in upstate New York despite severe rain. Fences collapsed; the event became de facto free. 32 acts performed — Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, The Who, Santana, Creedence Clearwater Revival, Joan Baez. Two people died (one from an overdose, one crushed by a tractor); two babies were born. The festival became the defining symbol of the 1960s counterculture.
events.revealBlurb: August 15-18, 1969 — on Max Yasgur's farm in Bethel, NY. Hendrix closed at 9 AM Monday morning to a dwindling crowd with a distorted, feedback-laced "Star-Spangled Banner." The 1970 documentary won an Oscar.

events.title: Spotify Launches
events.blurb: A Swedish music-streaming service, developed in Stockholm and Stockholm alone for two years, launched invitation-only to users in six European countries. The service offered an enormous music library — eventually over 100 million tracks — free with ads or $10/month without. It would restructure the entire music business: album sales collapsed, streaming became the default, and royalties flowed through aggregation models that artists found miserly.
events.revealBlurb: October 7, 2008 — founded by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon. The service arrived in the U.S. in July 2011 after lengthy negotiations with major labels. It had 620 million monthly active users as of 2024 — the largest audio subscription service ever.

events.title: Alam Ara Released — India's First Talkie
events.blurb: Police were deployed outside Majestic Cinema in Bombay that afternoon because the crowds gathering to hear a Hindi film speak for the first time overwhelmed the streets. The fantasy-romance had seven songs, making it arguably the first Bollywood musical; screenings sold out continuously for eight weeks, and the print of the film has since been completely lost.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1931 — directed by Ardeshir Irani. The film was shot in just 40 days. Every surviving account describes the audience's shock at hearing dialogue emerge from the screen, many reportedly weeping.

events.title: Kalidas Released — First Tamil Talkie
events.blurb: A mythological musical about the Sanskrit poet Kalidasa opened at Kinema Central in Madras on Diwali and became simultaneously the first sound film in Tamil and the first in Telugu — the hero singing in Telugu, the heroine speaking Tamil, a third actor delivering dialogue in Hindi, making it a multilingual sound experiment disguised as a devotional drama.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1931 — directed by H.M. Reddy, just months after Alam Ara introduced sound to India. A young actor billed only as L.V. Prasad played a cameo; he would later become one of South India's most powerful film producers. The film is now preserved at the National Film Archive.

events.title: Bombay Talkies Founded
events.blurb: A studio established in Malad, Bombay, by a London-trained filmmaker and his aristocratic actress-wife drew European technical talent — German cameramen, British equipment — to build India's first modern film facility with synchronised sound stages and a Western-style star system. It launched the careers of Dilip Kumar, Ashok Kumar, and Madhubala within its first fifteen years.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1934 — founded by Himanshu Rai and Devika Rani. Rai died in 1940 while the studio was mid-production; Devika Rani, then 32, took sole control and ran it for another nine years. The studio was where a young Dilip Kumar walked in looking for work and was handed a contract he barely understood.

events.title: Zanjeer Released
events.blurb: After fifteen consecutive flops, a young actor was offered the role of an angry, incorruptible police inspector in a crime thriller that every major star of the decade — Dharmendra, Dev Anand, Rajesh Khanna — had turned down. The film's success redirected an entire industry's idea of what a Hindi film hero could look like: not romantic or comic, but furious.
events.revealBlurb: May 11, 1973 — written by Salim-Javed, directed by Prakash Mehra. Amitabh Bachchan was cast almost by elimination. Salim Khan and Javed Akhtar then wrote nearly every subsequent Bachchan blockbuster with him specifically in mind, insisting on his casting as a contractual condition.

events.title: KGF: Chapter 2 Released
events.blurb: A Kannada-language action sequel about a gold miner's violent rise and rule over an illegal mining empire released simultaneously in five languages, broke the opening-day records of every film before it in the Hindi belt, and became the first Kannada film to gross ₹1,000 crore — a moment that announced South Indian cinema's claim on the pan-India blockbuster market.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 2022 — directed by Prashanth Neel. KGF Chapter 1 had been a slow-burn cult hit two years earlier; the sequel was designed from the outset as the louder, bigger answer. Yash, who plays Rocky, was a regional star of modest fame before Chapter 1; after Chapter 2 he turned down a reported 50 offers in a single week.

events.title: Qutb-ud-Din Aibak Founds the Delhi Sultanate
events.blurb: A Turkic slave-soldier who had risen to command the armies of the Ghurid empire in India declared himself Sultan of Delhi after his master was assassinated in Central Asia. This man — who had been purchased as a child in a Nishapur slave market — now controlled the largest political entity in the subcontinent. He commissioned what would become one of India's most visited monuments, the Qutb Minar in Delhi, before dying four years later in a polo accident.
events.revealBlurb: 1206 CE — Qutb-ud-Din Aibak, first Sultan of Delhi. He was known as "Lakhbaksh" (giver of lakhs) for his generosity. The Qutb Minar he began stands 73 metres tall and remains the tallest brick minaret in the world over 800 years later.

events.title: Harihara and Bukka Found the Vijayanagara Empire
events.blurb: Two brothers from a family of provincial commanders — who had previously served both the Kakatiya and the Delhi Sultanate before being captured, converted, and then reportedly re-converted to Hinduism — established a new kingdom on the south bank of the Tungabhadra river. The city they built, Vijayanagara ("City of Victory"), grew into one of the largest in the medieval world, shielding South India's temple culture from northern incursions for two and a half centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 1336 CE — Harihara I and Bukka Raya I, Tungabhadra river, Karnataka. Today their capital is called Hampi — a UNESCO World Heritage Site of 1,600 monuments sprawled over 26 square kilometres of boulder-strewn landscape. Monkeys included at no extra charge.

events.title: Guru Nanak Is Born
events.blurb: A child was born to a Khatri family in a Punjab village that is now in Pakistan. At age 30, he reportedly vanished into a river for three days; when he emerged, he proclaimed "There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim" and began wandering across Asia — from Sri Lanka to Tibet to Baghdad — singing hymns about the oneness of the formless divine, the equality of all people, and the corruption of caste and ritual. He walked an estimated 28,000 kilometres in his lifetime.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1469 — Guru Nanak Dev Ji, born at Talwandi (now Nankana Sahib, Pakistan). His birthday is celebrated as Gurpurab on the full moon of Kartik. Nanak composed 974 hymns, which form the core of the Guru Granth Sahib — the living, eternal Guru of the Sikh faith.

events.title: Babur Wins the First Battle of Panipat
events.blurb: A Timurid prince from Fergana, having failed to hold Samarkand three times, led a force of 12,000 men and 15 cannons against the Delhi Sultanate's 70,000-strong army and 1,000 war elephants on a flat plain north of Delhi. Using a Central Asian tactic called the tulughma — flanking arcs of cavalry combined with cannon fire — he routed and killed the last Lodi sultan in a single afternoon, ending one dynasty and beginning another.
events.revealBlurb: April 21, 1526 — Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire. His cannons were among the first used on an Indian battlefield. The elephants, terrified by the sound, turned and trampled their own side. Babur wrote about it all in his memoirs, the Baburnama, with the eye of a poet.

events.title: Akbar Secures the Mughal Throne
events.blurb: A 13-year-old Mughal prince was crowned emperor at Kalanaur, Punjab, moments after his father fell down a library staircase in Delhi. His regent Bairam Khan immediately faced a formidable rival — the Hindu general Hemu, who had taken Delhi with 30,000 cavalry and 1,500 war elephants. At the second Battle of Panipat, Hemu was felled by a stray arrow mid-battle, his army collapsed, and the boy king's empire was saved.
events.revealBlurb: February 1556 CE — Akbar the Great. The same king who would later abolish the jizya tax, marry Rajput princesses, invent a syncretic religion, and reportedly have three thousand women in his harem started his reign as a frightened teenager hiding behind his general.

events.title: Brunelleschi's Dome Completed
events.blurb: A Florentine goldsmith turned architect completed, after 16 years of work without scaffolding, a vast octagonal dome over the crossing of a century-old cathedral. The double-shelled design, assembled with four million bricks in a self-supporting herringbone pattern, spanned 42 metres — wider than any dome built since Roman antiquity. The cathedral had stood domeless for over a century, waiting for someone to figure out how.
events.revealBlurb: August 25, 1436 — consecrated. Filippo Brunelleschi at Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence. He refused to leave blueprints, fearing competitors would steal the ideas. Part of the technique was rediscovered only in the 20th century through forensic study of the bricks.

events.title: Columbus Makes Landfall
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator commanding three vessels landed on an island in the present-day Bahamas after 70 days at sea, believing he had reached islands off the coast of Asia. He planted a royal standard, claimed the land in the name of the Spanish Crown, and named the island San Salvador — its indigenous inhabitants called it Guanahani.

events.title: Cabral Reaches Brazil
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Portuguese nobleman commanding a 13-ship expedition bound for India — following Vasco da Gama's recent route — sailed so far west to catch favourable trade winds that he accidentally made landfall on a South American coast later named after a dyewood tree. He claimed it for Portugal under the six-year-old Tordesillas line and continued on to India. The accidental detour is the conventional starting point of Brazilian history.
events.revealBlurb: April 22, 1500 — Pedro Álvares Cabral in modern Bahia. He called the land "Ilha de Vera Cruz." Some historians think the "accidental" landfall was deliberate, responding to intelligence Portuguese mariners had gathered earlier. He lost six ships and over 100 men to storms en route onward to India.

events.title: Magellan's Fleet Departs
events.blurb: Five ships and 270 sailors departed from Sanlúcar de Barrameda under a Portuguese navigator flying a Spanish flag, carrying provisions for two years. Three years later, one battered ship and 18 survivors returned — the first vessels to circumnavigate the globe, though their commander had been killed in a Filipino skirmish partway through.

events.title: Luther at the Diet of Worms
events.blurb: A 37-year-old German theologian, summoned to a Rhineland imperial assembly under a guarantee of safe conduct, was asked to recant his written attacks on papal authority. He asked for a day to consider; the next day he returned and refused unless shown his error from scripture. The emperor placed him under imperial ban the following month. He would have been executed if the elector of Saxony had not hidden him in a castle, where he translated the New Testament into German.
events.revealBlurb: April 17-18, 1521 — Martin Luther before Holy Roman Emperor Charles V. The famous line "Here I stand; I can do no other" may be apocryphal; it appeared only in a printed account issued after the events. Luther lived another 25 years, marrying, fathering six children, and publishing prolifically.

events.title: Army-McCarthy Hearings
events.blurb: A televised congressional inquiry pit a grandstanding senator against the U.S. Army, which he had accused of harboring subversives. Over 36 days, 20 million Americans watched live as his bullying tactics eroded public sympathy. The defining moment came when a quiet Boston lawyer turned to him and asked, "Have you no sense of decency, sir?"
events.revealBlurb: April 22 to June 17, 1954 — the lawyer was Joseph Welch. His line came on June 9, after McCarthy attacked a young associate. Six months later the Senate voted 67-22 to censure McCarthy. He drank himself to death within three years.

events.title: Khrushchev Secret Speech
events.blurb: Speaking to a closed session of the Soviet Communist Party's 20th Congress, a new premier delivered a four-hour denunciation of his predecessor's personality cult, show trials, and mass purges. The text was supposed to remain secret but leaked within months, shattering communist movements worldwide and launching a partial cultural thaw at home.
events.revealBlurb: February 25, 1956 — Nikita Khrushchev, three years after Stalin's death. A Polish journalist smuggled the text to Israeli intelligence, who gave it to the CIA. Millions of Soviet prisoners were rehabilitated in the following years.

events.title: Hungarian Revolution
events.blurb: A student demonstration in Budapest grew within hours into a nationwide uprising against a Moscow-backed government. For twelve days, a reform-minded premier announced democratic elections and withdrawal from the eastern bloc military alliance. Then 2,500 Soviet tanks rolled into the country, crushing the revolt and killing some 2,500 Hungarians.
events.revealBlurb: October 23 to November 10, 1956 — reform premier Imre Nagy was tricked into a "negotiation," arrested, and secretly executed two years later. 200,000 Hungarians fled west. The West's failure to intervene exposed the limits of containment.

events.title: Bay of Pigs Invasion
events.blurb: A brigade of 1,400 Cuban exiles, trained and armed by the CIA, landed on a remote beach on their home island hoping to spark a popular uprising against its revolutionary government. Promised U.S. air support was withheld at the last moment. Within three days all the invaders were dead or captured. A young American president took public responsibility for the fiasco.
events.revealBlurb: April 17-20, 1961 — Kennedy, in office just three months, had inherited the plan from Eisenhower. His approval rating actually rose afterward; he quipped, "the worse I do, the more popular I get." The captured exiles were ransomed for $53 million in food and medicine.

events.title: Fall of Saigon
events.blurb: As enemy tanks crashed through the iron gates of the presidential palace in a Southeast Asian capital, U.S. helicopters lifted the last embassy staff and thousands of desperate local allies from rooftops around the city. The image of the final Huey ascending from an apartment building became the defining photograph of a failed 20-year war. Within hours, the city was renamed after a revolutionary leader who had died six years earlier.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1975 — the city became Ho Chi Minh City. The evacuation, Operation Frequent Wind, removed 7,000 people by helicopter in 19 hours. The famous "last helicopter" photo actually shows a CIA staff house, not the embassy.

events.title: Fall of France
events.blurb: German armoured divisions crossed a forested highland deemed impassable by military doctrine, bypassed the most elaborate fixed defences in Europe, and in six weeks forced the capitulation of a nation whose army was considered the strongest on the continent. An armistice was signed in the same railway carriage used for the previous war's peace.
events.revealBlurb: May 10 – June 22, 1940. The armistice was signed at Compiègne in Hitler's deliberate reversal of the 1918 Armistice humiliation — he had the original railway carriage brought out of a museum. France lost 92,000 killed in six weeks. A junior general named de Gaulle flew to London and refused to accept the result.

events.title: Doolittle Raid on Tokyo
events.blurb: Sixteen medium bombers took off from the pitching deck of an aircraft carrier 650 miles out at sea — far beyond the designed launch range — and struck the enemy's capital and four other cities in daylight, causing minimal physical damage but shattering the belief that the home islands were invulnerable to aerial attack.
events.revealBlurb: April 18, 1942 — Lieutenant Colonel Jimmy Doolittle led 16 B-25 Mitchells off USS Hornet. None of the aircraft had enough fuel to land at friendly bases; crews ditched in China or the Soviet Union. Of 80 raiders, 3 were killed in the attacks and 8 were captured by Japan — 3 of those were executed.

events.title: Battle of the Coral Sea
events.blurb: Two opposing fleets manoeuvred for days without either side's surface ships ever sighting the other, their aircraft flying hundreds of miles over open ocean to find and strike carriers whose decks they could not see. One navy lost a fleet carrier and the other lost a light carrier — but the strategic consequence was that an invasion convoy turned back.
events.revealBlurb: May 4–8, 1942 — the first naval battle in history fought entirely by aircraft. Neither fleet's ships came within sight of the other. Japan lost the light carrier Shōhō; the US lost USS Lexington. The two Japanese fleet carriers damaged at Coral Sea were then unavailable at Midway — a fact that proved decisive a month later.

events.title: Warsaw Ghetto Uprising
events.blurb: On the eve of a major Jewish holiday, lightly armed fighters inside an urban ghetto launched a sustained armed resistance against a force sent to complete its deportation to killing centres — holding out for nearly a month against SS troops, armoured vehicles, and systematic building-by-building destruction before the last pockets were overcome.
events.revealBlurb: April 19 – May 16, 1943. The ZOB fighters had roughly 220 pistols, several dozen rifles, and a small supply of grenades and Molotov cocktails. SS commander Jürgen Stroop demolished the Great Synagogue of Warsaw as a symbolic finale on May 16, declaring: "The Jewish quarter of Warsaw is no more." He was hanged in Warsaw in 1952.

events.title: Italy's Armistice Announcement
events.blurb: A radio broadcast by a head of government announced that his country had signed an armistice with the opposing alliance, pulling out of an axis it had helped found, leaving its former partner's forces — which had already occupied key positions across the country — to decide how to respond. German forces immediately disarmed Italian troops and occupied cities across the peninsula.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1943 — Marshal Badoglio's broadcast at 7:42 PM. The armistice had actually been signed on September 3 but was kept secret. German Operation Achse activated within hours, disarming and capturing roughly 650,000 Italian soldiers. Many were sent to German labour camps; some 50,000 died in captivity. The king and Badoglio fled Rome before dawn.

events.title: Britney Shaves Her Head
events.blurb: A 25-year-old American pop star walked into a Los Angeles hair salon at 8 PM, asked a stylist to shave her head completely, and when the stylist refused, picked up the electric clippers and did it herself. Paparazzi captured the scene through the salon window. Images went global within hours, becoming an emblem of a period of intensely public personal struggle — divorce, custody battles, reportage, and tabloid harassment. She would be placed under conservatorship nine months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 16, 2007 — Britney Spears at Esther's Haircutting Studio, Tarzana, CA. The conservatorship lasted 13 years, ending in November 2021 after the #FreeBritney movement. Her 2023 memoir "The Woman in Me" describes the head-shaving as a reaction to feeling over-managed and pressured by the industry.

events.title: Michael Jackson Dies
events.blurb: A 50-year-old American singer widely regarded as the most successful pop star of his generation died of cardiac arrest at his rented Los Angeles home while preparing for a 50-concert comeback tour in London. His personal physician was later convicted of involuntary manslaughter for administering propofol, a surgical anesthetic, to help him sleep. His death prompted an outpouring of grief that crashed major websites and sold over 35 million of his records in the following six months.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 2009 — Michael Jackson. His physician, Conrad Murray, was sentenced to 4 years and served 2. His public memorial on July 7 drew 31 million U.S. TV viewers. The "This Is It" concert film, compiled from rehearsal footage, grossed $261 million posthumously.

events.title: Hamilton Opens on Broadway
events.blurb: A hip-hop-based musical about the founding-era American politician Alexander Hamilton, written by a 35-year-old playwright-composer who had performed an early version at a White House poetry event in 2009, opened on Broadway after a sold-out off-Broadway run. The show's casting of non-white actors as the Founding Fathers, its rapid-fire rap-through-historical-politics, and its grand storytelling about ambition and legacy made it a generational phenomenon. Tickets sold on the secondary market for over $1,000.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 2015 — Lin-Manuel Miranda as Hamilton at the Richard Rodgers Theatre. The show won 11 Tony Awards in 2016 and a Pulitzer Prize for Drama. A professionally filmed version premiered on Disney+ on July 3, 2020 during the COVID pandemic, drawing enormous viewership.

events.title: Prince Dies
events.blurb: A 57-year-old American musician was found unresponsive in an elevator at his Paisley Park estate and recording studio outside Minneapolis, having died alone of an accidental fentanyl overdose. He had been taking painkillers for chronic hip pain aggravated by decades of acrobatic stage performances. His catalogue — 39 studio albums, countless B-sides and unreleased tracks — was so extensive that new material continued to surface from his vault for years after his death.
events.revealBlurb: April 21, 2016 — Prince Rogers Nelson. He had no valid will; the distribution of his $156 million estate involved his six siblings and took six years of litigation to resolve. The tribute concerts in the weeks after his death included a Saturday Night Live special and coverage on every major music broadcast.

events.title: Notre-Dame Fire
events.blurb: A fire that began in the attic of an 850-year-old Gothic cathedral on an island in the Seine at the heart of Paris burned for nine hours, collapsing the 93-metre 19th-century spire and destroying two-thirds of the roof. Firefighters managed to save the main stone structure, the two bell towers, the three great rose windows, and most of the interior artworks. Notre-Dame's silhouette without its spire, broadcast live to the world, became a modern visual shock.
events.revealBlurb: April 15-16, 2019 — cause never conclusively determined; probably an electrical fault or a discarded cigarette. French President Emmanuel Macron pledged to reopen the cathedral within five years; it reopened December 7, 2024, more or less on schedule.

events.title: Johnstown Flood
events.blurb: After days of heavy rain, a poorly maintained earth dam built to create a private lake for a Pennsylvania hunting club gave way, releasing 20 million tons of water onto the steel-mill town 23 kilometres downstream. The wall of water reached speeds of 65 km/h and was 18 metres high. It killed 2,209 people in 10 minutes.
events.revealBlurb: May 31, 1889 — Johnstown, Pennsylvania. The hunting club's members (including Andrew Carnegie and Henry Clay Frick) were never successfully sued. The flood launched the American Red Cross onto the national stage; Clara Barton ran relief operations for five months.

events.title: Hurricane Katrina
events.blurb: A Category 3 hurricane made landfall on the US Gulf Coast, driving a storm surge that overtopped and breached the levee system protecting a major port city lying largely below sea level. 80 percent of the city flooded; 1,392 people died. The chaotic federal response — images of thousands stranded on a sports stadium roof, bodies floating in water — inflicted lasting damage on the administration in power.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 2005 — New Orleans, Louisiana. The Superdome housed 30,000 evacuees for five days in deteriorating conditions. The head of FEMA, Michael Brown, had previously run the International Arabian Horse Association; he resigned within two weeks.

events.title: Eyjafjallajökull Eruption
events.blurb: A glacier-capped volcano in Iceland erupted, sending a plume of fine silicate ash into the jet stream. Authorities across Europe, uncertain about engine safety, grounded all commercial aviation for six days. Around 10 million passengers were stranded, and global airlines lost an estimated $1.7 billion. Few people died, but the event showed how fragile modern mobility had become.
events.revealBlurb: April 14-20, 2010 — Iceland. The volcano's name became a running joke for newscasters. Stranded travelers included heads of state on their way to a funeral in Poland; many drove for days to get home. Rental car companies had their biggest week ever.

events.title: Deepwater Horizon Spill
events.blurb: A blowout on a semi-submersible drilling rig in the Gulf of Mexico killed 11 workers and severed the riser pipe to a well 1,500 metres below the surface. Over the next 87 days, as engineers tried increasingly improbable methods to cap it, roughly 780 million litres of crude oil gushed into the sea — the largest accidental marine oil spill in history.
events.revealBlurb: April 20, 2010 — off Louisiana. The well was finally killed in mid-September. BP paid over $65 billion in settlements, fines, and cleanup. A live-stream of the ocean-floor plume was watched by millions during the crisis; executives who claimed it was "relatively tiny" became memes.

events.title: Maui Wildfires
events.blurb: High winds from a distant hurricane drove grass fires through a historic town on a Hawaiian island, reaching speeds that outpaced emergency alerts. 102 people died — many trapped in cars attempting to flee along a single coastal road — in the deadliest US wildfire in over a century. The 19th-century whaling-era town of Lāhainā, once the kingdom capital, was almost completely destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: August 8, 2023 — Lāhainā, Maui. The outdoor warning siren network, the largest in the world, was never activated. Some survivors escaped by jumping into the Pacific Ocean and treading water for hours. Downed Hawaiian Electric lines were identified as the likely ignition source.

events.title: Founding of Rome
events.blurb: According to Roman tradition, Romulus killed his twin brother Remus in a quarrel over the city's walls, then became the first king of a settlement of seven hills beside the Tiber. Varro, working backward from consular lists, calculated the exact date centuries later and Rome adopted it as its birthday, celebrating it annually with the Parilia festival.
events.revealBlurb: April 21, 753 BCE — the traditional date. Romulus allegedly populated his new city by opening it as a sanctuary for fugitives, runaway slaves, and exiles. When women were in short supply, he invited the neighbouring Sabines to a festival and had his men abduct their daughters.

events.title: Publication of the Twelve Tables
events.blurb: A commission of ten patricians spent two years drafting Rome's first written legal code onto twelve bronze tablets displayed in the Forum, covering debt, inheritance, property rights, and family law. The code was a concession to plebeian demands that laws stop being secret knowledge monopolised by priestly and aristocratic insiders.
events.revealBlurb: 450 BCE, Rome. Every Roman schoolboy was required to memorise the Twelve Tables for generations afterward. One clause specified that a debtor who couldn't pay could be cut into pieces by his creditors — though historians debate whether this was ever actually carried out.

events.title: Gallic Sack of Rome
events.blurb: Senone Gauls under their chieftain Brennus routed a Roman army at the Allia River, then entered a largely deserted Rome three days later and burned it for seven months. The sole holdout was the Capitoline Hill, where a sacred flock of geese allegedly woke the defenders when a Gallic night-assault crept up the cliffs.
events.revealBlurb: July 390 BCE, traditional (Polybius says 387). The ransom Brennus demanded in gold was agreed, but the Romans protested he was using rigged weights. Brennus reportedly threw his sword onto the scales and bellowed "Vae victis" — "Woe to the vanquished."

events.title: Licinian-Sextian Laws
events.blurb: After a decade of plebeian obstruction that left Rome with no consuls at all, the tribunes Gaius Licinius Stolo and Lucius Sextius Lateranus forced through three laws: one relieving debt, one limiting landholding to 500 iugera, and one requiring that at least one consul each year be a plebeian. Lucius Sextius duly became the first plebeian consul in 366 BCE.
events.revealBlurb: 367 BCE, Rome. Licinius and Sextius blocked every other piece of legislation for ten straight years to force the patricians to negotiate — essentially inventing the political hostage tactic of governmental gridlock.

events.title: Edict of Milan
events.blurb: Emperors Constantine and Licinius met in Mediolanum and issued a joint agreement granting every person in the empire freedom to worship any deity they chose — ending official persecution of Christians and ordering the return of all property confiscated from them. It was not technically an edict and did not make Christianity the state religion, but it permanently changed the empire's religious landscape.
events.revealBlurb: February 313 CE. The document was addressed to governors as a letter, not proclaimed as a formal edict — scholars still debate its exact legal form. Licinius, who co-signed it, was himself a pagan; Constantine had him killed ten years later.

events.title: Mosaic Browser Released
events.blurb: Undergraduate students at a University of Illinois supercomputing centre released a graphical web browser for Unix, with a version for Windows and Mac released later in the year. Unlike the earlier terminal-based browsers, it could display images inline with text. Within 18 months, web traffic had grown by 10,000 percent. The browser's lead developer would leave to co-found a company that would dominate the next phase.
events.revealBlurb: April 22, 1993 — developed at the NCSA, lead developer Marc Andreessen. Andreessen co-founded Netscape within a year. Mosaic was free for non-commercial use, a decision that gave the web the critical mass it needed.

events.title: Google Incorporated
events.blurb: Two Stanford PhD students filed articles of incorporation for a search-engine company they had been developing in a dormitory and a rented garage in suburban California. Their algorithm, unlike those of competitors, ranked pages by how many other pages linked to them. They would never graduate. Their search index contained 60 million pages when they incorporated; it contains hundreds of billions today.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 1998 — Larry Page and Sergey Brin. The name is a misspelling of "googol," the mathematical term for 10^100. Their initial financial backer, Sun Microsystems co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim, wrote a $100,000 check to "Google Inc." before the company formally existed.

events.title: iTunes Store Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched an online music store selling individual songs for 99 cents each, a pricing decision its CEO had to personally negotiate with record-label executives deeply suspicious of any further internet disruption. The store sold a million downloads in its first six days. Within four years, it was the largest music retailer in the United States.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 2003 — Apple. Steve Jobs had threaten to "pull the plug" on the negotiations at one point. The catalogue launched with 200,000 songs, Mac-only; Windows compatibility came in October. The per-song price model reshaped the music industry.

events.title: Ellen's Oscar Selfie
events.blurb: A television talk-show host hosting the annual U.S. film industry awards ceremony staged an elaborate star-packed selfie live on stage, tweeting it from her Samsung phone. The image was retweeted more than a million times within an hour, temporarily breaking the social network. The photo included thirteen people — three winners, seven nominees, two non-nominees, and the show's host. It held the record for most-retweeted photo for years.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 2014 — Ellen DeGeneres at the 86th Academy Awards. The selfie was actually taken by Bradley Cooper. Samsung had paid $20 million for product placement on the telecast; arguably worth every dollar.

events.title: TikTok Launches Globally
events.blurb: A Chinese short-video company merged its existing lip-sync-focused app Musical.ly, acquired the previous year, into a new global brand — effectively introducing mainland China's most popular short-video format to Western audiences. The app's algorithm would prove uniquely good at inferring what content users wanted without asking them. Within three years, TikTok had over a billion users and had reshaped every other social platform's product roadmap.
