events.revealBlurb: August 2, 2018 — ByteDance merges Musical.ly into TikTok. By 2020, U.S. users were spending more time per day in TikTok than in Instagram or Facebook. President Trump attempted to ban it in 2020; the Biden administration attempted to force a U.S. divestment in 2024.

events.title: Iliad and Odyssey Composed
events.blurb: Oral-tradition epic poems about a mythic ten-year siege of a city in western Anatolia and the homecoming of a Greek king after it, composed or consolidated by a blind Ionian bard — or a school of bards working in his name — were set to writing for the first time, probably by scribes who took them down from live recitation. They would become the foundation texts of Greek literature, education, and religion.
events.revealBlurb: c. 750 BCE — traditionally ascribed to Homer. The "Homeric question" — whether one poet, many poets, or an oral tradition produced them — is still unresolved. The war they describe may reflect faint memory of Bronze Age conflicts around the archaeological site of Troy.

events.title: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales
events.blurb: An English civil servant in his mid-fifties died leaving unfinished a collection of stories told by pilgrims riding from Southwark to a Kentish cathedral shrine. Written in Middle English rather than French or Latin, the work demonstrated the poetic range of the English vernacular across a social spectrum — knights, millers, cooks, pardoners, the famously bawdy Wife of Bath. Only 24 of a planned 120 tales were ever completed.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1400 — Geoffrey Chaucer. He is often called the father of English literature. Roughly 80 manuscripts survive; the earliest complete ones date from the 1410s. The Wife of Bath's Tale became an early feminist touchstone.

events.title: Paradise Lost Published
events.blurb: A blind 58-year-old English poet, dictating to a rotating cast of scribes, completed a 10-book (later 12-book) epic poem retelling the Biblical account of the fall of man from the perspective of a sympathetically characterized Satan. Having narrowly escaped execution for his political writings under the restored monarchy, he was paid ten pounds for the manuscript. It would become the template for English epic poetry.
events.revealBlurb: 1667 — John Milton. He had gone blind in 1652 from untreated glaucoma. His daughters had to be taught to read — including Hebrew, Greek, and Latin — just so they could transcribe his dictations. "The mind is its own place..." is from Book I.

events.title: War and Peace Published
events.blurb: A 41-year-old Russian aristocrat completed the last serial installment of a vast historical novel following five aristocratic families through Russia's Napoleonic Wars. The finished work ran over 1,200 pages and combined personal drama, military history, and a 200-page essay on the philosophy of history tacked onto the end. The author rewrote the opening sentence at least seven times.
events.revealBlurb: 1869 — Leo Tolstoy. It was serialized in the journal Russky Vestnik between 1865 and 1869. Tolstoy later disowned most of his fiction on religious grounds and decades later attempted to destroy his own estate's copyright to prevent his heirs from profiting.

events.title: To Kill a Mockingbird Published
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Alabama-born New York airline reservation clerk published her first and, for over half a century, only novel — a semi-autobiographical story narrated by a six-year-old white girl whose father, a small-town Southern lawyer, defends a Black man falsely accused of raping a white woman. The book won a Pulitzer the next year and has been a school-curriculum fixture in the U.S. ever since.
events.revealBlurb: July 11, 1960 — Harper Lee. Her childhood friend Truman Capote was the model for the character Dill. Gregory Peck won an Oscar for the film adaptation. Lee published a second novel, "Go Set a Watchman," in 2015, a year before her death; it was an earlier draft of the same book.

events.title: Sputnik 1 Orbital Launch
events.blurb: A polished aluminum sphere the size of a beach ball lifted off from a steppe launch site and became the first human-made object to orbit Earth. Weighing 83 kilograms and trailing four whip antennas, it circled the planet every 96 minutes and broadcast a radio beep on 20 and 40 MHz audible to amateur operators worldwide for 22 days until its batteries died.
events.revealBlurb: October 4, 1957 — Sputnik 1. It carried zero scientific instruments; the entire payload was a thermometer and a radio transmitter. The beep's rhythm changed with cabin temperature, which meant the world's most-tracked signal was also the world's first space weather report.

events.title: First Space Station Launched
events.blurb: The Soviet Union placed the world's first space station, Salyut 1, into low Earth orbit using a Proton rocket. The 18.9-metre station provided a pressurized working volume of 90 cubic meters across three interconnected compartments and was designed to host rotating crews arriving by Soyuz capsule for extended scientific work.
events.revealBlurb: April 19, 1971 — Salyut 1. The station's only successful resident crew — Soyuz 11 — spent 23 days aboard, setting a spaceflight endurance record. All three died during reentry when a faulty valve vented the cabin to vacuum; they were found in their seats, un-suited. The disaster prompted a redesign requiring all cosmonauts to wear pressure suits during docking.

events.title: Hubble Space Telescope Launch
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Discovery deployed the Hubble Space Telescope into a 612 km orbit, positioning a 2.4-meter primary mirror above Earth's atmosphere to capture ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light without atmospheric distortion. The primary mirror was later found to have been ground 2.2 micrometers too flat — a spherical aberration correctable only by a servicing mission.
events.revealBlurb: April 24, 1990 — STS-31. The mirror flaw came from a testing lens installed backward by 1.3 mm. Three years later, astronauts installed corrective optics during the first Hubble servicing mission — essentially fitting the telescope with contact lenses. Hubble has since produced more than 1.5 million observations.

events.title: Mir Space Station Deorbit
events.blurb: Russia deliberately deorbited the Mir space station after 15 years of continuous operation, using three burns from a docked Progress cargo spacecraft to lower its orbit until it reentered the atmosphere over the South Pacific. Most of the station burned up during reentry, but approximately 1,500 kg of debris survived and splashed into the ocean between Australia and Chile.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2001 — Mir deorbit. Mir had been in orbit so long that cosmonauts reported the walls were alive with mold. A Russian company sold pay-per-view rights to watch the reentry from a chartered aircraft. Japan offered to purchase and keep the station operational; the deal fell through over cost. It had been visited by 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations.

events.title: Water Confirmed on the Moon
events.blurb: India's Chandrayaan-1 Moon Impact Probe detected spectral signatures consistent with water molecules during its 25-minute controlled descent to the lunar south pole, with readings from a mass spectrometer increasing steadily as the probe flew toward higher latitudes. Three instruments on the orbiting spacecraft corroborated the finding, confirming that water ice is present across the lunar surface.
events.revealBlurb: November 14, 2008 — Chandrayaan-1/MIP. The probe was decorated with the Indian national flag and crashed intentionally near Shackleton Crater at 85° south — making India the fourth nation to place an object on the Moon. The water discovery reversed decades of scientific consensus that the Moon was bone dry, reshaping plans for every future lunar base concept.

events.title: Radioactivity Discovered
events.blurb: A French physicist studying uranium salts placed a wrapped photographic plate in a drawer alongside a uranium sample during several cloudy days, expecting to run a sunlight experiment later. When he developed the plate anyway, he found a sharp image — proving the uranium was spontaneously emitting invisible radiation with no external energy source, a phenomenon no existing theory could explain.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1896 — Henri Becquerel announced to the Academy of Sciences that the image was "very distinct." The discovery was accidental: bad weather cancelled his planned sunlight experiment. He initially thought it was a variant of X-rays; it took the Curies to show radioactivity was a property of the atom itself.

events.title: Electron Announced
events.blurb: During a lecture at a London scientific institution, a physicist announced that cathode rays were composed of particles roughly one-thousandth the mass of a hydrogen atom — the first demonstration that atoms were not the smallest units of matter. The particles were initially called "corpuscles"; the modern name came from a suggestion by an Irish physicist the same year.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1897 — J.J. Thomson's discovery won him the Nobel Prize in 1906, and his son George Thomson won a separate Nobel in 1937 for proving the electron was a wave. Father and son together proved it was a particle and a wave — one of physics' neatest family rivalries.

events.title: Penicillin Discovered
events.blurb: Returning from vacation, a bacteriologist noticed a petri dish of Staphylococcus bacteria had been contaminated by a mold that had dissolved the surrounding bacterial colonies into clear halos. He cultured the mold — Penicillium notatum — and determined it produced a substance lethal to bacteria, naming it penicillin.

events.title: DNA Double Helix Published
events.blurb: A two-page letter in the journal Nature described a double-helical structure for deoxyribonucleic acid, with two chains running in opposite directions held together by hydrogen bonds between paired bases. The authors noted their structure immediately suggested a mechanism by which genetic information could be copied.
events.revealBlurb: April 25, 1953 — Watson and Crick, aided by Rosalind Franklin's unpublished X-ray diffraction image known as "Photo 51". Their famous closing line: "It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing we have postulated immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism" — one of science's great understatements.

events.title: Pulsars Discovered
events.blurb: A graduate student mapping the sky with a radio telescope noticed a repeating pulse of radio waves arriving with uncanny regularity every 1.33 seconds — far too precise to be natural noise. The signal was briefly nicknamed "LGM-1" (Little Green Men) until other examples were found across the sky, establishing a new class of rapidly rotating neutron stars more accurate than any clock then built.
events.revealBlurb: November 28, 1967 — Jocelyn Bell Burnell spotted the anomaly in paper chart rolls she had to check by hand. Her supervisor Antony Hewish and astronomer Martin Ryle shared the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery; Bell Burnell was excluded despite being the one who found it, in what became one of science's most-debated Nobel omissions.

events.title: Lost Premieres
events.blurb: A serialized drama from ABC premiered its first episode — a 92-minute pilot for which the network had spent $14 million, then the most expensive pilot in TV history. A passenger jet crashes on a mysterious Pacific island; the survivors discover polar bears, giant submerged statues, smoke monsters, and hatches. The show pioneered the era of densely plotted serialized TV that viewers would parse online week by week, and ran for six increasingly contested seasons.
events.revealBlurb: September 22, 2004 — ABC, creators J.J. Abrams, Damon Lindelof, Jeffrey Lieber. Cast included Matthew Fox, Evangeline Lilly, Josh Holloway, and Jorge Garcia. The finale on May 23, 2010 drew 13.5 million viewers and a generation-defining debate over whether it had all made sense.

events.title: William and Kate Wedding
events.blurb: The 28-year-old second-in-line heir to the British throne married his 29-year-old university sweetheart at Westminster Abbey in London before a congregation of 1,900 and a global TV audience estimated at 2 billion. The bride wore a long-sleeved ivory lace gown; the couple kissed twice on the Buckingham Palace balcony. The marriage, closely followed by the British tabloids for years, has so far produced three children and remained notably less turbulent than the equivalent royal marriage of the generation before.
events.revealBlurb: April 29, 2011 — Prince William and Catherine Middleton. William succeeded his father Charles as Prince of Wales when Charles became king in September 2022. Their three children, in line to the throne: George (2013), Charlotte (2015), Louis (2018).

events.title: Osama bin Laden Killed
events.blurb: A team of US Navy SEALs, helicoptered into the Pakistani city of Abbottabad at night, stormed a walled compound where the founder of al-Qaeda had been hiding for over five years, 1.3 kilometres from Pakistan's premier military academy. He was killed in the raid, along with four others. His body was buried at sea from a US carrier to prevent his grave becoming a pilgrimage site. The president announced the operation in a late-night television address; crowds gathered outside the White House chanting "USA."
events.revealBlurb: May 2, 2011 — Operation Neptune Spear. SEAL Team Six; President Barack Obama. Bin Laden had orchestrated the September 11, 2001 attacks. His death ended a 9-year, 8-month manhunt. The compound was demolished months later by the Pakistani government.

events.title: Ice Bucket Challenge
events.blurb: A viral social-media fundraising campaign for ALS — amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, commonly called Lou Gehrig's disease — swept the internet over the summer. Participants filmed themselves dumping a bucket of ice water on their heads, challenged friends to do the same, and donated to an ALS charity. Celebrities from Bill Gates to Donald Trump to LeBron James participated. The campaign raised $115 million for ALS research over two months and funded the discovery of a significant ALS-related gene.
events.revealBlurb: Peak: August 2014. The campaign was co-founded by Pete Frates, an ALS patient who died of the disease in 2019. The ALS Association estimated $230 million in total donations. Subsequent research identified the NEK1 gene as a contributor to ALS, directly attributable to the challenge funds.

events.title: "The Dress" Goes Viral
events.blurb: A 21-year-old Scottish woman posted a photograph of a dress on her Tumblr account asking for help settling a family argument — was it black and blue, or white and gold? The photo went viral overnight. Approximately 40 percent of viewers saw it as white and gold; 50 percent as black and blue. Vision scientists spent months examining why. The actual dress, in real life, was black and blue. The phenomenon became a landmark case study in how individual visual perception varies based on assumptions about ambient lighting.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 2015 — Cecilia Bleasdale's photograph, posted by Caitlin McNeill. Roman Originals, who made the dress, saw a 560 percent spike in sales. Neuroscientists published papers on it for years. It revived serious research into color constancy and top-down visual processing.

events.title: Botticelli's Primavera
events.blurb: A Florentine painter completed a large poplar panel for the bedroom of a Medici cousin, depicting nine mythological figures in a grove of orange trees — Venus at the centre, the Three Graces dancing, a gusting wind god chasing a nymph who is transformed into the flower-bearing goddess of spring. It is among the first Renaissance paintings to take mythological (not religious) subject matter on its own terms.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1482 — Sandro Botticelli. The painting contains at least 500 identifiable plant species, some 190 different flowers. Botticelli was later nearly destroyed by Savonarola's movement and reportedly burned some of his own work in the bonfire of the vanities.

events.title: Dürer's Self-Portrait
events.blurb: A 28-year-old German painter and printmaker completed a small panel depicting himself facing the viewer head-on, with long centre-parted hair and his right hand raised in a gesture traditionally reserved for depictions of Christ. It was a provocative piece of self-fashioning — the artist as holy creator. The inscription beside his head, dated to the year, pointed out how few European painters had ever signed their own faces.
events.revealBlurb: 1500 — Albrecht Dürer. Now in Munich's Alte Pinakothek. Dürer's German contemporaries thought the pose bordered on blasphemous. The picture has been read as the first true self-portrait-as-self-expression in Western art.

events.title: Leonardo da Vinci Dies
events.blurb: A 67-year-old Florentine polymath died in a small château in the Loire Valley, where the French king had invited him to retire. On the easel beside his bed was an unfinished portrait of a Florentine merchant's wife that he had carried with him for sixteen years and never delivered to the man who had commissioned it. The king would acquire the painting from his executor; the subject's name, Lisa Gherardini, would eventually become the most famous name in art.
events.revealBlurb: May 2, 1519 — Leonardo at Clos Lucé, Amboise. The portrait is the Mona Lisa, now in the Louvre, which he had begun around 1503. He bequeathed his notebooks, which he wrote in mirror script, to his assistant Francesco Melzi.

events.title: Hokusai's Great Wave
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Japanese printmaker produced the first of thirty-six woodblock prints depicting views of a sacred mountain, all showing it from different perspectives and in different weather. The first print, which viewers sometimes mistook for the title piece, showed an enormous wave curling in threatening foam over three small fishing boats, with the mountain a distant cone between its spray. The distinctive blue pigment, Prussian blue, was a recent European import.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1831 — Katsushika Hokusai. The print is one of the most widely reproduced images in the world; thousands of impressions survive. Hokusai called himself "the old man mad about drawing" and claimed he would become a true artist only at 110.

events.title: Duchamp's Fountain
events.blurb: A French artist submitted an ordinary porcelain urinal, signed with a pseudonym and dated, as a sculpture entitled "Fountain" to the first exhibition of New York's Society of Independent Artists. The Society's board — of which he was a member — voted after heated debate to reject it. He resigned in protest. The original object was lost; the artist authorized 17 replicas over subsequent decades, each now valued at millions.
events.revealBlurb: April 1917 — Marcel Duchamp, signed "R. Mutt 1917." The original was photographed by Alfred Stieglitz and then disappeared. A 2004 survey of 500 art-world professionals named it the most influential artwork of the 20th century. An artist attacked a replica with a hammer in 2006.

events.title: Raja Harishchandra Released
events.blurb: A mythological silent film about the legendarily truthful king Harishchandra — shot in Bombay using an all-male cast because no actress would agree to appear on screen — opened at the Coronation Cinematograph in Girgaon and became India's first feature film, running 3,700 feet of hand-cranked footage. Its creator had spent over a year learning to develop film himself after being refused laboratory access.
events.revealBlurb: May 3, 1913 — Dadasaheb Phalke's debut. He was a printer by trade. Legend says he watched The Life of Christ (1906) in Bombay and decided India needed its own screen mythology. All the female roles were played by male wrestlers and cooks; no respectable woman would work in pictures.

events.title: First Filmfare Awards Ceremony
events.blurb: A British-origin film magazine inaugurated India's first popular film awards at Bombay's Metro Theatre with only five categories, winners chosen through postal ballot by readers, and a chief guest who was the US Ambassador to India. The trophy — a black-painted female figure — later became among the most recognisable objects in the entire industry and came to be known, simply, as the Black Lady.
events.revealBlurb: March 21, 1954 — then called the "Clare Awards" after a recently deceased film critic. Best Film went to Bimal Roy's Do Bigha Zamin; Dilip Kumar won Best Actor for Daag. The ceremony's postal-ballot system meant the public, not critics, decided the winners — a populist structure the awards kept for decades.

events.title: Bobby Released
events.blurb: A teen romance between a rich Hindu boy and a poor Goan Christian fisherman's daughter — directed by a father launching his second son into stardom — upended Bollywood's existing template of adult romances and star-crossed melodrama. The film's bikini-clad poster and youth-coded aesthetics signalled an entirely new demographic that filmmakers had been ignoring.
events.revealBlurb: September 29, 1973 — Raj Kapoor directing Rishi Kapoor in his leading-role debut, opposite Dimple Kapadia in hers. The film became the highest-grossing of 1973. Raj Kapoor cast Dimple Kapadia after seeing her at a party; she was sixteen. She married Rajesh Khanna five months after filming wrapped.

events.title: Taare Zameen Par Released
events.blurb: A film about an eight-year-old with undiagnosed dyslexia shipped off to boarding school for failing every subject — told largely from the child's hallucinatory perspective — earned ₹98 crore worldwide and prompted school boards across India to introduce dyslexia screening. Its child lead, discovered through an open casting call, had never acted before.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2007 — Aamir Khan's directorial debut, having taken over from Amole Gupte mid-production. Darsheel Safary, then 9, auditioned among 1,000 children. The film catalysed new Indian legislation on learning disability accommodation in schools. Khan dedicated the film to every child who had been misunderstood.

events.title: Baahubali: The Conclusion Released
events.blurb: The sequel to a Telugu fantasy epic that had left an entire nation debating one question — "Kattappa ne Baahubali ko kyun mara?" — opened to the largest advance booking in Indian cinema history, sold over 10 million tickets in its first weekend, and earned ₹1,000 crore net in India faster than any film before it, definitively crossing the barrier that only Hindi cinema had previously approached.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 2017 — directed by S.S. Rajamouli. The two-part production cost ₹430 crore, still the most expensive Indian film made at the time. The "why" answer to the Kattappa question — withheld for two years — turned its release into a cultural event rather than just a premiere.

events.title: St. Paul's Cathedral Completed
events.blurb: After 35 years of construction replacing a medieval cathedral destroyed in the Great Fire of London, a 68-year-old English architect watched his son install the final piece of his new cathedral's lantern atop its dome — the first cathedral anywhere in the world to have been entirely designed, built, and completed by a single architect within his own lifetime. The triple-domed design, inspired by St. Peter's in Rome, rose 111 metres above the City of London.
events.revealBlurb: 1710 — Sir Christopher Wren. He also designed 52 other London churches after the Great Fire of 1666. He was buried in the cathedral's crypt when he died in 1723 at 90; his memorial reads "Si monumentum requiris, circumspice" — if you seek his monument, look around you.

events.title: Suez Canal Opens
events.blurb: The French-designed 193-kilometre sea-level canal linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea — dug largely by corvée (unpaid forced) Egyptian labour over ten years with massive loss of life — opened to international traffic. A procession of 68 ships led by a French imperial yacht sailed from Port Said to the Red Sea over four days. The canal cut the sea route from London to Bombay by about 7,200 kilometres and shifted the geography of global trade.
events.revealBlurb: November 17, 1869 — designer Ferdinand de Lesseps. Giuseppe Verdi's opera Aida, commissioned by Khedive Ismail for the opening, arrived too late and premiered in 1871. The canal was nationalized by Egypt in 1956, triggering the Suez Crisis.

events.title: Empire State Building Opens
events.blurb: A 381-metre, 102-story skyscraper opened in Manhattan, having been designed in two weeks and constructed in just 410 days — often at a rate of 4.5 stories per week. It displaced the Chrysler Building as the tallest building in the world and held that title for 41 years. The Great Depression left it mostly empty for its first decade; New Yorkers nicknamed it the "Empty State Building." It entered profit in 1950.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1931 — architect William F. Lamb (Shreve, Lamb and Harmon). The B-25 bomber that crashed into the 79th floor in heavy fog on July 28, 1945 killed 14 people but damaged the structure only moderately. King Kong famously climbed it in the 1933 film.

events.title: Channel Tunnel Opens
events.blurb: A 50-kilometre twin-bore railway tunnel under the English Channel opened, linking France to Britain below the sea floor for the first time in 8,000 years. The tunnel had been proposed repeatedly since the early 19th century but had always been shelved on defensive grounds; the end of the Cold War and European integration finally made it buildable. Construction had involved eleven tunnel-boring machines drilling simultaneously from both sides; the breakthrough was within 35 centimetres alignment.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1994 — Queen Elizabeth II and President François Mitterrand cut a ribbon jointly. Total project cost: £9 billion, roughly 80 percent over budget. The tunnel is used by Eurostar passenger trains and the freight-carrying Shuttle. Trains reach 160 km/h underground.

events.title: Burj Khalifa Opens
events.blurb: A 828-metre tapering skyscraper — Y-shaped in plan, with a buttressed central core — opened in a Gulf financial center as the tallest building in the world, dramatically taller than the previous record holder. Its construction had begun at the height of a regional real-estate bubble; by opening it had lost over 60 percent of its value and been taken over by a neighbouring emirate, after whose ruler the tower was hastily renamed. Its name had been "Burj Dubai" during construction.
events.revealBlurb: January 4, 2010 — architect Adrian Smith at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. The renamed "Burj Khalifa" honored Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan of Abu Dhabi, whose government bailed out Dubai during the financial crisis. Tom Cruise dangled from the outside in "Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol" (2011).

events.title: Washington's First Inauguration
events.blurb: George Washington took the presidential oath of office on the balcony of Federal Hall in New York City, becoming the first executive of the new constitutional republic and establishing by his conduct nearly every precedent of the American presidency — from the two-term norm to the cabinet system to the title "Mr. President." He was the unanimous choice of the Electoral College, the only president ever to achieve that distinction.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1789 — Federal Hall, New York City. Washington reportedly added "so help me God" to the oath, though historians dispute this. He was so anxious about the job that he wrote to a friend he felt like a culprit going to execution. He almost certainly didn't want a second term either.

events.title: Louisiana Purchase Treaty Signed
events.blurb: American negotiators in Paris signed a treaty acquiring roughly 828,000 square miles of territory from France — doubling the size of the United States — for approximately $15 million, or about three cents per acre. The purchase, which Napoleon offered because he needed cash for his European wars, encompassed all or part of fifteen future states and opened the continent to westward expansion.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1803 — Paris. Jefferson had only authorized $10 million and was seeking to buy New Orleans alone; Napoleon offered the entire territory. Jefferson privately wondered whether he had constitutional authority to make the deal at all, but bought it anyway. The full price, with interest, came to about $23 million.

events.title: Apollo 11: First Humans on the Moon
events.blurb: At 10:56 pm EDT that evening, astronaut Neil Armstrong stepped off the lunar module Eagle onto the surface of the Moon and became the first human being to walk on another world, watched live by an estimated 600 million people — roughly one-fifth of humanity. Buzz Aldrin joined him 19 minutes later; the two planted an American flag, collected samples, and departed after 2 hours and 31 minutes on the surface.
events.revealBlurb: July 20, 1969 — Sea of Tranquility, the Moon. Armstrong's famous line was supposed to be "one small step for a man" — he swears he said it; the transmission dropped the "a." Michael Collins orbited alone overhead for 21 hours while his crewmates were on the surface. President Nixon had a speechwriter prepare a statement in case they didn't make it back.

events.title: Watergate Break-In
events.blurb: At 2:30 in the morning, Washington D.C. police arrested five men inside the headquarters of the Democratic National Committee at the Watergate complex, where they had broken in to photograph documents and plant surveillance devices. The burglars were connected to the Committee to Re-Elect the President, and the discovery of the break-in and the subsequent cover-up by the Nixon White House eventually destroyed his presidency.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1972 — Watergate complex, Washington, D.C. The burglars were caught because a security guard noticed tape on a door latch and called the police. Nixon won re-election in November 1972 in one of the largest landslides in American history — 520 to 17 electoral votes — while the cover-up was already underway.

events.title: Obergefell v. Hodges: Same-Sex Marriage Nationwide
events.blurb: The Supreme Court held 5–4 that the Constitution guarantees same-sex couples the right to marry, requiring all 50 states to issue marriage licenses and recognize same-sex unions performed elsewhere. Justice Anthony Kennedy's majority opinion grounded the right in both the Due Process and Equal Protection clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment.
events.revealBlurb: June 26, 2015 — Washington, D.C. The case's lead plaintiff, Jim Obergefell, had sought only to have his name listed on his deceased husband's death certificate as the surviving spouse. When the ruling was announced, the White House was illuminated in rainbow colors that night.
